name: data-description
content:
Plain-text English passages, one boundary each. The paths below are relative to the root of the mounted competition data. Locate that root by name rather than hard-coding it, as shown under *Loading the data*.

## What you get

| Path | Samples | Labels | Use it to |
|---|---:|:---:|---|
| `dataset/train/` | 1,221 | yes | train or fine-tune your method |
| `dataset/dev/` | 380 | yes | self-score locally before spending a submission |
| `dataset/test_public/` | 760 | **no** | the passages you predict and submit |
| `models/bge-base-en-v1.5/` | — | — | the only permitted pretrained encoder |
| `solution.py` | — | — | a runnable baseline you can start from |
| `sample_submission.csv` | 760 rows | — | the exact expected submission schema |

The three splits are disjoint: no id appears in more than one, so `dev` is a genuine held-out estimate.

The 760 rows in `test_public` combine the two hidden evaluation sets. Kaggle scores **380 of them on the Public Leaderboard** and the other **380 on the Private Leaderboard**, which decides the final ranking. You submit predictions for all 760 and cannot tell which row belongs to which. All splits are drawn from the same distribution, so your `dev` score is a reasonable estimate of your leaderboard score.

## On-disk format

```text
dataset/train/data.jsonl          {"id": "...", "text": "..."}
dataset/train/answers.jsonl       {"id": "...", "boundary_char_index": 1842}
dataset/dev/data.jsonl            {"id": "...", "text": "..."}
dataset/dev/answers.jsonl         {"id": "...", "boundary_char_index": 1790}
dataset/test_public/data.jsonl    {"id": "...", "text": "..."}   <- no answers
models/bge-base-en-v1.5/          the encoder, load from disk
```

One JSON object per line. Ids in `answers.jsonl` match ids in the corresponding `data.jsonl`.

## Loading the data

Do not hard-code paths. Kaggle mounts competition data under `/kaggle/input/competitions/<competition-slug>/`, the slug differs per fork, and the nesting can change. The supplied `solution.py` locates files by name:

```python
def find_input(name, search_root="/kaggle/input"):
    matches = sorted(Path(search_root).rglob(name))
    if not matches:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{name} not found under {search_root}")
    return matches[0]

dataset = find_input("dataset")
model_dir = find_input("bge-base-en-v1.5")
```

The model has no internet access at run time, so `bge-base-en-v1.5` must be loaded from that local directory rather than by hub id.

# OFFICIAL COMPETITION RULES

**ENTRY IN THIS COMPETITION CONSTITUTES YOUR ACCEPTANCE OF THESE OFFICIAL COMPETITION RULES.**

The Competition named below is a skills-based competition intended to promote and further the field of data science and machine learning.

You must register through the Competition Website to enter. To participate, you must agree to these Official Competition Rules, which incorporate by reference the provisions and content of the Competition Website and any Competition-Specific Rules stated below (collectively, the “Rules”).

Please read these Rules carefully before entering the Competition. By entering, participating, or making a Submission, you confirm that you have read, understood, and agreed to these Rules.

These Rules form a binding agreement between each Participant and the Competition Sponsor with respect to the Competition.

All Submissions must comply with the requirements stated on the Competition Website and in these Rules. Submissions will be evaluated using the evaluation metric described on the Competition Website.

This Competition does not offer monetary or non-monetary prizes.

You may not participate in the Competition or make Submissions using more than one Kaggle account.

---

# 1. COMPETITION-SPECIFIC TERMS

## 1.1 Competition Title

IOAI 2026 - Ghost of the Machine

## 1.2 Competition Sponsor

IOAI 2026 - Kazakhstan

## 1.3 Competition Sponsor Address

Kazakhstan, Astana

## 1.4 Competition Website

https://ioai2026.kz/

## 1.5 Prizes

No monetary or non-monetary prizes are offered in this Competition.

## 1.6 Participation Format

The Competition is open to individual Participants and AI Models track Participants only.

Teams, team formation, and team mergers are not permitted.

## 1.7 Submission Format

This is a notebook-based competition.

All valid Submissions must be generated by a Kaggle Notebook associated with the Competition.

Participants must submit through the notebook-based submission workflow specified on the Competition Website.

Direct upload of prediction files or other competition outputs is not permitted.

The submitted notebook must generate the required submission file in the format specified on the Competition Website.

## 1.8 Data and Model Restrictions

Participants may use only:

1. the Competition Data provided by the Competition Sponsor; and
2. the pretrained models explicitly provided by the Competition Sponsor, and any models that ship inside a permitted Python package itself.

No other external data, pretrained models, model weights, checkpoints, embeddings, or externally generated information may be used. In particular, models that would need to be downloaded at runtime are not permitted, and the notebook has no Internet access.

Participants may not attach datasets, models, or other resources that they created themselves and that are not part of the Competition Data.

Solutions are not required to use machine learning. Any legitimate method that solves the task is permitted, including search-based and algorithmic approaches. A solution is not legitimate if it attempts to obtain unauthorised access to validation or test data, or otherwise circumvents the Competition platform.

### Hardware

Participants may use either a CPU notebook or a single T4 GPU:

- CPU: `"enable_gpu": false` and `"machine_shape": ""`
- GPU: `"enable_gpu": true` and `"machine_shape": "NvidiaTeslaT4"`

Selecting `NvidiaTeslaT4` provisions two T4 GPUs, but Participants must use only **one** of them, by setting the device to `cuda:0`. This maintains parity with the main IOAI competition, where students receive a single GPU slice with comparable memory.

`NvidiaTeslaP100` must not be used.

---

# 2. COMPETITION-SPECIFIC RULES

In addition to any applicable general Kaggle competition rules, Participants understand and agree to the following Competition-Specific Rules.

## 2.1 Individual Participation

a. Participants must compete individually.

b. Teams are not permitted.

c. Team formation and team mergers are not permitted.

d. A Participant may use only one Kaggle account to enter or participate in the Competition.

e. Sharing private code, private solutions, private predictions, or private competition results between Participants is not permitted.

---

## 2.2 Submission Requirements

a. All valid Submissions must be created and submitted through a Kaggle Notebook associated with the Competition.

b. Direct upload of locally generated prediction files is not permitted.

c. The submitted notebook must generate the required competition output file in the location and format specified on the Competition Website.

d. A Submission may be rejected or disqualified if:

1. it was not generated through the required notebook workflow;
2. it uses prohibited data, models, weights, or external resources;
3. it does not comply with the required submission format;
4. it cannot be reproduced from the submitted notebook and permitted resources; or
5. it otherwise violates these Rules.

e. The submitted notebook must contain the code necessary to reproduce the corresponding Submission.

f. Final submitted notebooks must run with Internet access disabled.

---

## 2.3 Submission Limits

a. A Participant may create a maximum of fifteen (15) Kaggle Notebook versions for this Competition.

Each `kaggle kernels push` creates one Notebook version and counts towards this limit, whether or not the run succeeds and whether or not the resulting version is submitted to the Competition. A version that fails, errors, or is stopped at the runtime cap still counts.

A Notebook version may be submitted to the Competition at most once.

Kaggle's platform counters track submissions to the Competition rather than Notebook versions, so this limit is not enforced automatically by the Kaggle system. It is enforced by the Competition organizers.

b. Final Submissions are auto-selected by the system on the basis of Public Leaderboard score. Participants are not required to, and should not, select Final Submissions manually through the Kaggle web interface.

c. All Submission limits are applied individually to each Participant.

d. Each Kaggle Notebook run associated with a Submission must not exceed a
maximum runtime of six hundred (600) seconds, i.e. ten (10) minutes.
Participants are responsible for enforcing this limit themselves by passing
the `--timeout 600` flag to `kaggle kernels push`, as described on the
Competition Website under "Kaggle CLI Submission".

---

## 2.4 Competition Timeline

Competition dates, including the Start Date, Entry Deadline, Final Submission Deadline, and any other applicable deadlines, are shown on the Competition Website under the Competition Timeline.

Participants are responsible for ensuring that all required actions and Submissions are completed before the applicable deadlines.

A Submission counts only if the `kaggle competitions submit` command is sent **before** the Final Submission Deadline. Metric scoring may finish after the deadline; that is permitted. A Submission sent after the deadline is still accepted by Kaggle and still receives a score, but it does not appear on the Leaderboard and does not count towards final ranking.

Participants are advised to submit several minutes before the deadline to allow for platform latency.

---

## 2.5 Competition Data

### a. Permitted Use

Participants may access and use the Competition Data only for:

1. Participating in this Competition;
2. Developing and evaluating solutions for this Competition; and
3. Discussing the Competition on the official Kaggle competition forums.

The Competition Data may not be used for unrelated purposes unless the Competition Sponsor explicitly grants separate permission.

### b. Data Security

Participants must use reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent access to the Competition Data by persons who have not formally agreed to these Rules.

Participants may not transmit, duplicate, publish, redistribute, sell, sublicense, or otherwise make the Competition Data available to any person who is not authorized to access it.

Participants must notify Kaggle and the Competition Sponsor upon becoming aware of any unauthorized access, disclosure, or distribution of the Competition Data.

Participants agree to cooperate in addressing any unauthorized access or distribution.

---

## 2.6 External Data, Models, and Tools

### a. External Data Is Prohibited

Participants may not use any data other than the Competition Data provided by the Competition Sponsor.

Prohibited external data includes, but is not limited to:

1. public datasets;
2. private datasets;
3. purchased datasets;
4. manually collected external data;
5. web-scraped data;
6. data obtained through external APIs;
7. externally sourced labels;
8. external metadata;
9. retrieval databases or external knowledge bases;
10. data generated or enriched using information not included in the Competition Data.

### b. Only the Provided Pretrained Model Is Allowed

Participants may use only the pretrained model explicitly provided by the Competition Sponsor. For this Competition that model is **bge-base-en-v1.5**, a text encoder supplied with the Competition Data and loaded from its local directory.

No other pretrained model may be used.

Prohibited resources include, but are not limited to:

1. external pretrained models;
2. external model weights;
3. external checkpoints;
4. externally trained adapters;
5. externally trained LoRA weights;
6. external embeddings;
7. external feature representations generated by another pretrained model;
8. external foundation models;
9. external large language models;
10. external vision models;
11. external audio models;
12. external multimodal models.

Participants may not replace, combine, ensemble, or supplement the provided pretrained model with any other pretrained model.

### c. Fine-Tuning

Participants may fine-tune or otherwise adapt the provided pretrained model using only the Competition Data, unless the Competition Website states otherwise.

Any additional model parameters, adapters, checkpoints, or derived weights created by a Participant must be produced using only:

1. the provided pretrained model; and
2. the Competition Data.

### d. External AI Services and APIs

Participants may not use external AI services or APIs to generate:

1. predictions;
2. labels;
3. features;
4. embeddings;
5. training data;
6. validation data;
7. synthetic competition data; or
8. other information used by the submitted solution.

This includes external hosted model APIs and inference services.

### e. Software Libraries

Participants may use generally available software libraries and programming tools, provided that those tools do not introduce prohibited external data, pretrained models, weights, checkpoints, or other restricted resources.

A software package that automatically downloads or includes a pretrained model may not be used unless that model is the specific pretrained model provided by the Competition Sponsor.

---

## 2.7 Internet Access

a. Final submitted notebooks must run with Internet access disabled.

b. A submitted notebook may not download data, model weights, checkpoints, packages containing prohibited pretrained resources, or other external information during execution.

c. All resources required by the final Submission must be included among the Competition resources or otherwise explicitly approved by the Competition Sponsor.

d. Use of Internet access to bypass the Competition’s restrictions on external data or external models is prohibited.

---

## 2.8 Automated Machine Learning Tools

Automated machine learning tools may be used only if they fully comply with all Competition restrictions. This includes only using libraries on the allowed list.

In particular, an automated machine learning tool must not:

1. access external data;
2. use external pretrained models;
3. download external model weights;
4. call external AI APIs;
5. introduce external features or embeddings; or
6. otherwise use resources prohibited by these Rules.

The Participant remains fully responsible for ensuring that every component used by the tool complies with these Rules.

---

## 2.9 Eligibility

Unless otherwise stated on the Competition Website or prohibited by applicable internal policies, employees, interns, contractors, officers, and directors of the Competition Sponsor, Kaggle, and their respective parent companies, subsidiaries, and affiliates may participate.

The Competition Sponsor may determine that certain individuals are not eligible for official ranking or recognition where participation would create a conflict of interest.

All Participants are responsible for complying with applicable laws, regulations, employer policies, and institutional policies.

---

## 2.10 Final Ranking and Reproducibility

a. Final rankings will be determined according to the evaluation metric and final-submission procedure described on the Competition Website.

b. The Competition Organizers may review a top-ranked Participant’s submitted notebook to confirm compliance with these Rules.

c. A top-ranked Participant may be required to provide:

1. the final submitted notebook;
2. training code;
3. inference code;
4. configuration files;
5. dependency information;
6. a description of the computational environment;
7. a description of the methodology;
8. preprocessing details;
9. training details;
10. hyperparameters; and
11. any other information reasonably necessary to reproduce the Submission.

d. The submitted solution must be reproducible using only:

1. the Competition Data;
2. the permitted pretrained model;
3. permitted software libraries; and
4. the code and resources included in or permitted for the submitted notebook.

e. A Participant may be disqualified from the final ranking if:

1. the Submission cannot be reproduced;
2. prohibited external data was used;
3. a prohibited pretrained model or external model resource was used;
4. the submitted notebook does not generate the claimed Submission;
5. the Participant refuses to provide reasonably required reproducibility information; or
6. the Participant otherwise violates these Rules.
7. This list is not exhaustive.

f. If a Participant is disqualified, the Competition Sponsor may adjust the final rankings accordingly.

---

## 2.11 No Prizes or Compensation

a. This Competition does not offer monetary prizes.

b. This Competition does not offer non-monetary prizes.

c. Participation does not create any right to payment, compensation, employment, contract work, reimbursement, or other financial benefit.

d. Participants are responsible for their own costs associated with participating in the Competition.

---

## 2.12 Intellectual Property

a. Except for rights expressly granted under these Rules or the Kaggle platform terms, Participants retain ownership of their original code and other original materials created for the Competition.

b. Participants remain responsible for ensuring that they have the right to use any software libraries or other permitted resources included in their Submission.

c. Participants may not include material in a Submission if its license or terms of use prevent the Participant from complying with these Rules.

d. Nothing in these Rules grants a Participant ownership of:

1. the Competition Data;
2. the provided pretrained model; or
3. other materials supplied by the Competition Sponsor.

e. Any additional licensing requirements for submitted solutions must be stated separately and clearly on the Competition Website.

---

## 2.13 Compliance Review

The Competition Sponsor may review any Submission for compliance with these Rules.

The Competition Sponsor may request reasonable evidence showing:

1. how the Submission was created;
2. what data was used;
3. what model or models were used;
4. how the provided pretrained model was used;
5. what software dependencies were used; and
6. whether the submitted notebook reproduces the Submission.

Failure to provide sufficient information may result in disqualification.

---

## 2.14 Governing Law

Unless otherwise stated in the Competition-Specific Rules, claims arising out of or relating to these Rules will be governed by California law, excluding its conflict-of-laws rules, and will be litigated exclusively in the federal or state courts of Santa Clara County, California, USA.

The parties consent to personal jurisdiction in those courts.

If any provision of these Rules is held to be invalid or unenforceable, all remaining provisions will remain in full force and effect.

---

# 3. KEY DEFINITIONS

For purposes of these Rules:

**Competition Data** means all data officially provided by the Competition Sponsor for use in the Competition.

**Competition Sponsor** means the organization or individual identified in Section 1.2.

**External Data** means any data or information not included in the Competition Data.

**Participant** means an individual registered to participate in the Competition.

**Permitted Pretrained Model** means only the specific pretrained model identified in Section 1.8 and Section 2.6.

**Submission** means a competition entry generated and submitted through the required Kaggle Notebook workflow.

**Submitted Notebook** means the Kaggle Notebook version used to generate a Submission.

**Competition Website** means the official Kaggle competition page identified in Section 1.4.

name: abstract
content:
# Ghost of the Machine

- **Time limit:** 600 seconds (10 minutes) per run
- **Environment:** one T4 GPU (~16 GB VRAM) or CPU, no internet
- **Notebook versions:** 15 maximum
- **Solution size:** 1 MB
- **Storage:** 5 GB
- **Pretrained models:** only `bge-base-en-v1.5`, a text encoder, supplied with the competition data
- **Baseline score:** 28.60 Public

Strange things are happening at the National Archive of Kazakhstan. Librarians say that some books used to end differently, but no one can prove it, because every copy is the same and every story still makes sense. You are invited as an AI researcher to locate the changes.

Each passage begins as human-written text and silently switches, exactly once, to a continuation generated by a language model. The passage stays coherent throughout. Your task is to find the switch: the character index where the human part ends and the machine-generated part begins.

Submissions are made from a Kaggle notebook using the Kaggle CLI. See the **Kaggle CLI Submission** tab for the full flow, and **Description**, **Data** and **Evaluation** for the task itself.

name: Description
content:
Strange things are happening at the National Archive of Kazakhstan. Librarians say that some books used to end differently, but no one can prove it — every copy is the same, and every story still makes sense. You are invited as an AI researcher to locate the changes.

## Task

A passage begins as human-written text and, at some point, silently switches to a continuation generated by a language model. Read as a whole, it looks like one coherent piece, but somewhere in the middle the author changes from a person to a machine.

**Your task is to find that switch: the character index where the human part ends and the machine part begins.**

Each sample is a single string `text`. There is exactly one boundary. Everything before it is human; everything from it onward is machine-generated.

- **Part A** (before the boundary) is an excerpt of human-written text.
- **Part B** (from the boundary on) is a continuation produced by a language model, conditioned on Part A.
- Each side is at least 180 words; total length is roughly 500–800 words.

The label is `boundary_char_index`, the character offset where Part A ends:

```python
human_part   = text[:boundary_char_index]
machine_part = text[boundary_char_index:].lstrip()
```

## Allowed models

Exactly one pretrained model may be used, and it ships with the competition data:

- **bge-base-en-v1.5** — a 110M-parameter text **encoder** (embedding model). It produces sentence and passage embeddings; it is not a generative language model.

You may use it frozen as a feature extractor, or fine-tune it on the labelled `train` split. Full fine-tuning fits comfortably inside the memory and time budget.

Classical and statistical tools are unrestricted. You may build any feature-based model, for example a scikit-learn regressor, on top of embeddings you compute yourself. The restriction applies only to *pretrained deep-learning weights*.

No other pretrained weights, no external data, and no internet access during the graded run.

## Baseline

The supplied `solution.py` estimates a single number from the training set — the mean boundary position as a fraction of passage length — and applies it to every test passage. It scores **28.60** on the Public Leaderboard. It exists to demonstrate the interface, not to be competitive.

## Where to find everything

| Topic | Tab |
|---|---|
| Files, splits, and on-disk format | **Data** |
| Submission format and the metric | **Evaluation** |
| How to submit, limits, and runtime cap | **Kaggle CLI Submission** |
| Prompts for starting and continuing your agent | **Starter Prompt** / **Continuation Prompt** |
| The technical report you must write | **Report Generation Prompt** |

name: Scoring
content:
## Submission format

Write a file named `submission.csv` with exactly these columns, in this order:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `id` | sample id from `dataset/test_public/data.jsonl` |
| `boundary_char_index` | your predicted character offset, an integer |

Example:

```csv
id,boundary_char_index
example_001228,1790
example_001229,2450
```

Include exactly one row for every id in `test_public` (**760 rows**). Row order does not matter; rows are matched by `id`.

`boundary_char_index` must be an integer in `[0, len(text)]` and must be accepted by Python's `int()`. A missing id, a duplicate id, an unknown id, a non-integer value, or an out-of-range value scores 0 for that sample.

## Metric

For each sample, let `p` be your prediction and `t` the true boundary. The per-sample score decays exponentially with the character distance:

$$
\text{score} = \exp\left(-\frac{|p - t|}{\tau}\right) \in (0, 1], \quad \tau = 100
$$

This gives:

| Distance from the true boundary | Per-sample score |
|---:|---:|
| 0 characters (exact) | 1.00 |
| 25 characters | ≈ 0.78 |
| 50 characters | ≈ 0.61 |
| 100 characters | ≈ 0.37 |
| 500 characters | ≈ 0.01 |

The final score is the **mean of the per-sample scores over the split, multiplied by 100** and rounded to two decimal places. Higher is better, and the range is 0.00 to 100.00.

The metric rewards getting *close*, not only exact. Halving your average error is worth far more than occasionally hitting a boundary precisely.

## Public and private leaderboards

- **Public Leaderboard** (live during the competition): scored on 380 of the 760 test rows.
- **Private Leaderboard** (revealed at the deadline): scored on the other 380. This determines the final ranking.

You submit all 760 predictions and cannot tell which rows are which. A high public score does not guarantee a high private score, so avoid tuning against the public leaderboard.

For calibration: the supplied baseline scores **28.60** Public and **32.68** Private.

name: Kaggle CLI Submission
content:
This competition is **notebook-only**: predictions cannot be uploaded as a file. Every submission must come from a notebook that ran on Kaggle's servers. The steps below do that entirely from the command line.

## Limits for this competition

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Notebook versions | **15 maximum** |
| Kernel runtime | **600 seconds (10 minutes) maximum** |
| Concurrent CPU sessions | 5 |
| Concurrent GPU sessions | 2 |
| GPUs usable per run | **1** (set your device to `cuda:0`) |
| Internet in the notebook | Disabled |
| Solution source size | 1 MB |
| Team size | 1 |

### Capping the runtime at 600 seconds

You must cap every run at **600 seconds**. Kaggle does not enforce this for you, so pass `--timeout` on every push:

```bash
kaggle kernels push -p my-solution/ --timeout 600
```

`--timeout` takes **seconds**, so `600` is the 10-minute cap. The budget covers everything in the run: the offline package install, any training or fine-tuning you do, and inference on all 760 test passages.

A run killed at the timeout produces no usable `submission.csv`, so write the output file before the budget runs out. A long run is also a bad trade: with only 2 concurrent GPU sessions, a slow notebook buys you fewer iterations.

## The deadline rule

`kaggle competitions submit` must be **sent before the competition deadline**.

- Submit before the deadline, scoring finishes after it: **counts**.
- Notebook finished in time but you submit after the deadline: does not count.
- Notebook still running at the deadline: does not count.

Late submissions are still accepted and still produce a score you can see, but they never appear on the leaderboard. Aim to submit a few minutes early.

## Before you start

Accept the competition rules in your browser. There is no CLI equivalent, and data download fails until you do:

```text
https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/<competition-slug>/rules
```

Then install and authenticate the CLI:

```bash
pip install kaggle
export KAGGLE_API_TOKEN="KGAT_..."   # kaggle.com -> Settings -> API
```

## Step 1: Create the notebook folder

A notebook is a folder holding exactly two files:

```text
my-solution/
├── script.py
└── kernel-metadata.json
```

## Step 2: Attach the data in `kernel-metadata.json`

Your notebook has **no internet access**, so every input must be declared up front. There are two separate lists and you need both:

```json
{
  "id": "<your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug>",
  "title": "My Solution",
  "code_file": "script.py",
  "language": "python",
  "kernel_type": "script",
  "is_private": true,
  "enable_gpu": true,
  "enable_internet": false,
  "machine_shape": "NvidiaTeslaT4",
  "dataset_sources": ["kamalkhan/ioai-2026-wheel-dataset"],
  "competition_sources": ["<competition-slug>"],
  "kernel_sources": [],
  "model_sources": []
}
```

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| `dataset_sources` | Mounts the wheel dataset, which is how packages get installed offline |
| `competition_sources` | Mounts `dataset/`, `models/`, and the starter |
| `enable_internet` | Must stay `false` |
| `enable_gpu` + `machine_shape` | Both are needed for a GPU run. Use `NvidiaTeslaT4` |

For a CPU-only run, set `"enable_gpu": false` and `"machine_shape": ""`.

Selecting `NvidiaTeslaT4` provisions two T4 GPUs. Use only **one**, by setting your device to `cuda:0`. `NvidiaTeslaP100` must not be used; Kaggle's PyTorch build does not support it.

## Step 3: Write `script.py`

Start from the supplied `solution.py` in the competition data. Keep two things from it: the environment-setup block at the very top, unchanged, and the two helper functions `find_input` and `read_jsonl` that are defined below it. Replace only `predict_boundaries` and `main` with your own solution.

```python
# =============================================================================
# IOAI 2026 - Ghost of the Machine - TECHNICAL REPORT
# (8-10 paragraphs; see the "Report Generation Prompt" tab for the template)
# =============================================================================

# -- keep the starter setup block here, unchanged --
setup_ioai_env()

# -- keep these two helpers from solution.py --
# def find_input(name, search_root="/kaggle/input"): ...
# def read_jsonl(path): ...

# -- your solution below --
import csv, json
from pathlib import Path

dataset = find_input("dataset")
model_dir = find_input("bge-base-en-v1.5")   # the only allowed pretrained model

test_rows = read_jsonl(dataset / "test_public" / "data.jsonl")
print(f"passages to predict: {len(test_rows)}")

# ... build your model, predict one boundary index per passage ...


def predict(text):
    """Return the predicted boundary, an int in [0, len(text)]."""
    raise NotImplementedError("your model goes here")


out = Path("/kaggle/working/submission.csv")
with out.open("w", newline="") as fh:
    w = csv.writer(fh)
    w.writerow(["id", "boundary_char_index"])
    for row in test_rows:
        p = int(predict(row["text"]))
        if not 0 <= p <= len(row["text"]):
            raise ValueError("prediction out of range for " + row["id"])
        w.writerow([row["id"], p])

print(f"wrote {out} with {len(test_rows)} rows")
```

Four rules that cause most first-time failures:

- `setup_ioai_env()` must run **before** you import `torch`, `transformers`, or anything else it installs. `pip` cannot replace a module Python has already loaded, so an import above it silently keeps the old version.
- Write the output to `/kaggle/working/submission.csv` with the exact header `id,boundary_char_index`.
- Include **exactly one row per test id** (760 rows). Row order does not matter; rows are matched by `id`.
- Load `bge-base-en-v1.5` from its local directory. A hub id such as `"BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5"` triggers a download and fails, because the notebook has no internet.

## Step 4: Run the notebook on Kaggle

```bash
kaggle kernels push -p my-solution/ --timeout 600
```

Each push prints a version number. Record it; you need it to submit:

```text
Kernel version 3 successfully pushed.
```

Then wait for the run to finish:

```bash
kaggle kernels status <your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug>
```

Statuses go `QUEUED -> RUNNING -> COMPLETE` (or `ERROR`). Poll every ~15 seconds.

Concurrency limits apply across all your notebooks at once: **5** CPU sessions, **2** GPU sessions. Exceeding them rejects the push with `Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached`.

## Step 5: Check the output (optional but recommended)

```bash
kaggle kernels output <your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug> -p out/
```

This downloads `submission.csv` and the run log. Verify the row count (760) and the header before spending a submission. The log is also where you confirm the offline install worked:

```text
IOAI environment ready (wheels from /kaggle/input/datasets/...)
```

## Step 6: Submit

```bash
kaggle competitions submit <competition-slug> \
  -k <your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug> \
  -v <version-number> \
  -f submission.csv \
  -m "short description"
```

`-f submission.csv` is **not** a local file path. It names an output file that already exists in the completed notebook version on Kaggle. Nothing is uploaded from your machine.

Submitting does **not** re-run your notebook. It scores the `submission.csv` your run already produced. To change your predictions, push a new version and submit that.

## Step 7: Read your score

```bash
kaggle competitions leaderboard <competition-slug> --show
kaggle competitions submissions <competition-slug>
```

## Submission limits

**Your budget is 15 notebook versions.**

Every `kaggle kernels push` creates a version and spends one of the 15, even if the run fails, errors, or is stopped at the 600-second cap. Each version may be submitted to the competition at most once.

### `submission-limits` does not track your budget

`kaggle competitions submission-limits` reports a different quantity from the one that is limited here. It counts **submissions to the competition**; your budget is **notebook versions**. The two diverge in both directions:

```bash
kaggle kernels push -p my-solution/ --timeout 600
# creates a version, spends 1 of your 15
# submission-limits: UNCHANGED

kaggle competitions submit <competition-slug> -k <owner>/<slug> -v 3 -f submission.csv -m "..."
# submission-limits: decrements
```

So the counter can read a large remaining number while you have already spent most of your 15 versions. Track your own usage from the version numbers printed by each push.

Kaggle does not enforce the version limit. The competition organizers do.

Practical consequences:

- Do not push speculatively. A failed push is a spent version.
- Validate your script before pushing: check that it writes `/kaggle/working/submission.csv`, that the header is `id,boundary_char_index`, and that every prediction is an integer inside the passage.
- Self-score on `dataset/dev/` first. It is labelled, disjoint from the test set, and costs you nothing.
- Kaggle occasionally starts a run before the competition data has finished mounting, which fails with `FileNotFoundError`. Pushing again resolves it, but the retry spends another version. Locating files by name rather than by a hard-coded path avoids failures that merely look like this one.

## Report requirement

The script you submit should carry a short technical report in a comment block at the very top. See the **Report Generation Prompt** tab for the template. The report carries no score.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| Data download returns 403 or 404 | The account has not accepted the rules. Open the competition in a browser and click **Join competition**. There is no CLI equivalent. |
| `FileNotFoundError` on the first push after attaching the competition | The data mount was not ready. Pushing again resolves it, but costs another notebook version. |
| Old package versions despite the setup block | Something was imported above `setup_ioai_env()`. Move all such imports below it. |
| `Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached` | Wait for a running GPU session to finish, or use a CPU notebook. |
| Model fails to load / tries to download | Load `bge-base-en-v1.5` from the local path returned by `find_input`, not by hub id. |
| Score of 0 on some rows | The id was missing, duplicated, unknown, or the value was not an integer in range. |
| Submission accepted but absent from the leaderboard | It was sent after the deadline. Submit earlier next time. |
| Run stopped early with no `submission.csv` | It hit the 600-second cap. Reduce training time and write the output file before the budget runs out. |

name: Report Generation Prompt
content:
Every submitted script should carry a short technical report describing **the solution in that file**.

## What the report is for

- It carries **no score**. It does not affect your Public or Private Leaderboard position.
- It is a reference for your team and for the IOAI Jury if you need to appeal a score, since agent-written code can be hard to read.
- After the contest and after your redaction, the report is published alongside your de-anonymised score on the final leaderboard, for transparency.

## Where it goes

Inside a comment block at the **very top** of the script you submit, above the environment setup block.

## Length and focus

8-10 short paragraphs. Describe the **submitted solution to this task**, not your agentic system, harness, or prompting strategy.

## Prompt

Use this prompt to generate or refresh the report:

```text
Write the technical report for the solution in the script you are about to
submit. Place it as a comment block at the very top of that file, above the
environment setup block, following the template in "Report Generation Prompt".

Write 8-10 short paragraphs. Describe only the submitted solution: what it
does, why, and what you measured. Do not describe your agent, harness, or
prompting strategy. Be specific and quantitative wherever you can: name the
features, the hyperparameters, and the scores you observed.

If you tried approaches that did not make it into this file, say so briefly and
say why they were dropped. If something in the final solution is a known
weakness or was left unfinished, say that plainly.
```

## Template

```python
# =============================================================================
# IOAI 2026 - AI Models Track - Ghost of the Machine
# TECHNICAL REPORT
# =============================================================================
#
# 1. SUMMARY
#    One paragraph. What does this solution do, end to end, and what Public
#    Leaderboard score did it achieve?
#
# 2. APPROACH
#    How is boundary detection framed? For example: direct regression of the
#    character index, per-sentence or per-window classification followed by
#    argmax, change-point detection over an embedding sequence, or something
#    else. Say why this framing was chosen.
#
# 3. TEXT REPRESENTATION
#    How the passage is split and encoded. State whether bge-base-en-v1.5 is
#    used, whether it is frozen or fine-tuned, what unit is embedded (sentence,
#    fixed window, sliding window), and what other features are used.
#
# 4. TRAINING
#    What was trained, on what data, for how long. Give the split used, the key
#    hyperparameters, and the wall-clock training time inside the notebook. If
#    nothing was trained, say so.
#
# 5. FROM MODEL OUTPUT TO A CHARACTER INDEX
#    How a single integer boundary_char_index is produced per passage, and how
#    you guarantee it is an integer inside [0, len(text)].
#
# 6. RESULTS
#    Score on dataset/dev/, and the corresponding Public Leaderboard score.
#    Note any gap between them and your explanation for it.
#
```
